lead.text: *Twelve weekly briefings. One skill per week. One practice log, kept honestly.*
The 30-Day Program in the main appendices got you started. This program takes you through a full quarter — the shortest realistic window in which sustained change compounds into visible capability.

items: A BRIEFING — the concept and its practical application, in 5 minutes of reading.
A PRACTICE ASSIGNMENT — the specific thing you will do this week.
A REFLECTION PROMPT — the specific question to sit with at week's end.

lead.text: Do this program with a real notebook, paper or digital. The point is not to read the weeks. The point is to log the practice.

blocks.text: *Anchored in: Level 1.1*
THE BRIEFING

The single most important second in a professional life is the one between provocation and response. This week you install that second — as a physical, trainable habit, not a philosophical aspiration.

Everything else in this program builds on the quality of your response under pressure. If you cannot pause, no other technique will work when you most need it. If you can pause reliably, everything else becomes accessible.
The training is not to feel calm. It is to produce calm behavior even when the internal state is activated. Over months, the state and the behavior converge — but the behavior comes first.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Every morning: three cycles of inhale-4, exhale-6 before you touch your phone.
• When triggered by an email/message: run the 4-Breath Reset. Log it — date, trigger, what you did instead of reacting.
• Install a 30-second delay on all after-9pm sends.
• Draft one saved 'Pause Phrase' you can send when you need time to reply properly.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— How many times did I pause this week — and how many times did I react before I noticed?*
*— What is my most reliable physical trigger for activation? Where do I feel it in my body?*
*— Is there one specific relationship whose messages I still respond to reactively? What would change if I applied the Pause there?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“Two seconds of pause is worth two hours of damage control.”*
**WEEK 2**
*Anchored in: Level 1.2*
THE BRIEFING

You cannot regulate what you cannot name. This week you double the size of your emotional vocabulary, and thereby double your ability to respond to what you actually feel rather than to 'bad' or 'stressed.'

Research on emotional granularity (Lisa Feldman Barrett) shows that people who can name their emotions with more precision recover from bad states faster, cope better without unhealthy outlets, and make better decisions under pressure.
The training is a check-in ritual. Twice a day. One word. Not 'okay.' A specific word.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• 12 pm and 6 pm daily: pause for 30 seconds. Answer 'what am I feeling right now, and what is it about?' — with the most specific word you can find.
• Log every day for a week. Look for patterns.
• One difficult moment this week: apply the 6-4-2 method (family → flavor → about what).
• One conversation where 'fine' would normally have been your answer: give a genuine answer instead.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— What are the five specific emotions I felt most often this week?*
*— Which ones am I most in the habit of not naming?*
*— Was there a moment when naming an emotion accurately changed what I did next?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“If you can name it, you can work with it.”*
**WEEK 3**
*Anchored in: Level 1.3*
THE BRIEFING
You have a finite amount of attention per day. Most of it will be spent whether you decide consciously or not. The question is only whether you allocate it or drift.
This week: one 90-minute block per workday of genuine deep work. Not four. One. And the audit that reveals where the rest of your day actually goes.
You will discover that most of your working day is not doing what you thought it was doing. This is the first step to reclaiming it.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Book a 90-minute block in tomorrow's calendar. Then Wednesday. Then Friday.
• For those three days: phone in another room, notifications off, one specific task planned.
• Track outcomes: did I do it? Did I produce the intended output?
• One day this week, run the 3-Day Attention Audit structure — every interruption logged.
• Turn off notifications for the least-essential app on your phone. Notice if you miss it.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— In the deep-work block, what did I actually produce that I couldn't have produced in a fragmented day?*
*— What was my most surprising interruption pattern?*
*— What is one specific structural change I could make next week to protect my attention?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“Manage attention, not time. Time takes care of itself.”*
**WEEK 4**
*Anchored in: Level 1.5*
THE BRIEFING

You've spent three weeks changing your response, your vocabulary, and your attention. This week: the underlying operating layer — one habit built properly, so it survives the weeks when you don't feel like it.

The rule that matters: design for your worst self, not your best. The 2-minute version. The existing trigger. The 'never miss twice.' These are not compromises — they are what makes habits actually stick.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Pick ONE habit to build this week — chosen from the practices you've been trying in weeks 1–3.
• Define its 2-minute version. Not the aspirational version.
• Identify the existing habit you'll stack it to.
• Track daily: did I do it (yes/no). Nothing more.
• If you miss a day: do NOT double up. Just do it the next day.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— What was the 2-minute version I chose, and did I hit it every day?*
*— Where did I feel resistance — and what was actually happening in those moments?*
*— What would the 4-week version of this habit look like? Am I ready to keep going?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“Design for your worst self, not your best.”*
**WEEK 5**
*Anchored in: Level 2 (multiple lessons)*
THE BRIEFING
This week you install the thinking disciplines: define before solving, tag claims as F/S/I/O, ask one real question per meeting.
You do not become a sharp thinker by learning more frameworks. You become one by using a few specific moves in real time, in real conversations, until they become automatic.
The goal for the week: make three specific moves visibly better than you would have made them last month.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Every important message you receive this week: silently tag F/S/I/O before responding.
• In every meeting: ask exactly one real question from the 7-question ladder.
• Pick ONE recurring problem at work. Write out its 5-level problem statement. Notice: were you solving the right problem?
• One decision this week: catch a specific bias operating on you. Log it.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— Which of the 7 questions did I use, and which moment was most productive?*
*— Where did FSIO tagging change my response?*
*— Which bias did I catch operating on me — and what did I do about it?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“Sharp thinking is a small number of habits, practiced under pressure, until they become involuntary.”*
**WEEK 6**
*Anchored in: Level 3 (multiple lessons)*
THE BRIEFING
This week you practice the moves that turn 'I don't know' into 'I know how to find out.'
One 90-minute skill sprint. One well-designed ask. One time you refuse to guess and instead go find the primary source.
The point is not to master anything new. The point is to feel — in your body — the difference between drifting and figuring out.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Run one 90-minute skill sprint on something small you've wanted to learn.
• Send one four-line help request to someone whose input you actually need.
• One claim you've been repeating without checking: trace it to the primary source.
• One time you catch yourself stuck: run CODA-R before continuing.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— What did I learn this week that I could not have learned without deliberate design?*
*— Who did I ask, and what changed about the relationship after the ask?*
*— When did I stop searching and act — and was that the right stopping point?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“You don't need to know it. You need to know how to find out.”*
**WEEK 7**
*Anchored in: Level 4.1*
THE BRIEFING
This week you practice being visibly good at the single most under-practiced skill in professional life.
LMR: Listen, Mirror, Reflect. Applied to one real conversation per day. Consistently. Even when the content is boring or when you disagree.
The goal is not to be a therapist. The goal is to be the person people notice really heard them. That noticing is what changes relationships.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• One conversation per day: 5-second pause after they finish, then mirror 3–5 words, then a one-sentence reflection.
• In every meeting where someone speaks with emotion: label the emotion out loud. 'It sounds like you're worried about X.'
• One person you routinely half-listen to: give them one genuinely full-attention 15 minutes.
• One physical note this week: take handwritten notes during a consequential conversation.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— Which conversation changed most because I listened more carefully?*
*— Who told me something they hadn't planned to say?*
*— What did I hear that I would have missed if I had been drafting my reply while they spoke?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“Listen. Mirror. Reflect. Then decide what to say.”*
**WEEK 8**
*Anchored in: Level 4.3*
THE BRIEFING
This week you have ONE difficult conversation you have been putting off.
This is the hardest week of the program for most people. It is also the week where the biggest returns come from.
The rule: cheaper today than next month. Cheaper than the resentment you've been carrying. Cheaper than the version of the same conversation you'll eventually have to have anyway.
Book it. Prepare it. Have it.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Identify the one difficult conversation you've been avoiding most.
• Book time for it in the next 7 days.
• Write out the five-part structure the night before: purpose, your view, invite theirs, the third story, agree on next.
• Have the conversation. Reflect after.
• One additional harder move: give one piece of SBI-I feedback to someone this week.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— How did the conversation compare to what I feared?*
*— What did I hear from them that I hadn't anticipated?*
*— What am I now doing differently as a result?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“The hard conversation today is cheaper than the same conversation next month.”*
**WEEK 9**
*Anchored in: Level 5.1*
THE BRIEFING
This week you install the operational habit that quietly reshapes a working life: the Sunday 30 and the Top Three.
Not to become more productive. To become more deliberate. Most working professionals produce vast quantities of low-value output because they have never separated 'busy' from 'important.'
This week is when the machine of Level 5 starts turning.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Sunday evening: 30 minutes reviewing last week (what did I actually do?) and setting this week's Top Three.
• Book the Top Three into your calendar as 90-minute blocks.
• Each morning: 2-minute start on today's most important item before checking email.
• Friday: review — did I actually do them? What prevented me from what I couldn't complete?
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— What percentage of my week did the Top Three actually get?*
*— What competed for their time? Was that competition legitimate?*
*— What is the ONE structural change I could make next week to protect them better?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“If everything is a priority, nothing is.”*
**WEEK 10**
*Anchored in: Level 5.3, 5.6*
THE BRIEFING
This week you begin the shift from being the person who does the work to being the person who produces results — a shift that separates career trajectories more than any other single move.

The two moves: one proper delegation this week, with all five parts + reverse brief. And one piece of leverage built — a template, an automation, a documented process — for something you've done three or more times.
Most people never build leverage. The ones who do end up doing three times the work with less stress, and getting promoted twice as fast.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Delegate one task to a colleague or team member. Use all five parts. Get the reverse brief.
• Build one durable asset: a template, an SOP, an automation, or a shared knowledge document.
• Send it to two colleagues who could use it.
• Note the time it took, and estimate the time it will save you (and them) over the next 12 months.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— Where did my delegation break down — and what did I fail to specify?*
*— What is the highest-leverage system I could build next month?*
*— Am I still doing tasks that someone else could do with modest instruction? Which ones?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“Do it once. Note it twice. Systemize the third time.”*
**WEEK 11**
*Anchored in: Level 6 (multiple lessons)*
THE BRIEFING
Week 11 makes AI use a professional discipline rather than a novelty. This week you use AI meaningfully every workday, using the CGCEO-V structure and verification protocol.
The measure at week's end is not 'did you use AI a lot' — it is 'did you produce work you couldn't have produced alone, and did you verify it before relying on it?'
You will also begin your personal prompt library — the artifact that becomes part of your professional edge over years.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Every workday this week: at least one substantive AI-assisted task with a full CGCEO-V prompt.
• For every consequential AI output: run the verification checklist before relying on it.
• Save at least 5 prompts that produced exceptional output. Label them by use case.
• One difficult conversation or decision this week: use AI as a red-team or role-play partner before acting.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— Which AI-assisted task delivered the biggest return relative to my solo version?*
*— Where did verification catch a mistake? What was the mistake?*
*— What is the workflow I most want to build into a personal template based on this week?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“AI is a colleague on their first day. Give them context and check their work.”*
**WEEK 12**
*Anchored in: Level 7 & 8*
THE BRIEFING
The final week of the program is not about adding a new skill. It is about integrating the previous eleven and looking forward.

You will make one consequential decision using the Decision 7. You will run one pre-mortem on a live project. You will do the 10-year audit. And you will decide — deliberately — what practice from this program you will carry into the next quarter.
This is where the program becomes a permanent part of how you work rather than a training series you finished.
THIS WEEK'S PRACTICE

• Take one open decision. Run all seven questions in writing. Sleep on it. Decide.
• For one live project: run a full pre-mortem. Write the failure story. Extract the top 5 risks with owners.
• Do the 10-year audit questions: what will I wish I had spent more time on this year, less on, and what specific change will I make in the next 90 days?
• Choose ONE practice from the 12-week program that you will continue permanently. Design the 90-day version of it.
• Write a one-page letter to yourself, describing the person you were at the start of this quarter and the person you are at its end. File it. Read it in one year.
END-OF-WEEK REFLECTION

*— Which of the 12 weeks changed me most, and why?*
*— Which practice do I most want to carry forward — and what is the specific way I will keep it going without the structure of a program?*
*— What is the next 90-day project I choose to give this level of intention to?*
REMEMBER THIS
*“The book ends. Your practice does not.”*
**· CLOSING THE 12-WEEK PROGRAM ·**
Twelve weeks. Twelve briefings. Ninety days of deliberate practice.

If you did this program honestly — not perfectly, but honestly — you are a different professional than you were at week one. Not because you know new information. Because you have installed new habits, under real conditions, with real friction, and they have started to compound.

The next quarter is up to you. Some readers will restart the program with different emphases. Some will pick a single week and go deep on it for three months. Some will design their own program using this structure. All three are valid.
What matters is that a year from now you can look back and see that this quarter was not indistinguishable from the one before it. That is the only measure of a practice worth doing.
The Resourceful Human is not who you are. It is who you become — one week, one conversation, one difficult conversation, one small kept promise at a time.
Go do the work.
*— End of the 12-Week Program —*
